title: Quantum Energy Storage versus Heat-to-Work Conversion in an Interacting Spin System
authors: Omar Bachain, Mohamed Amazioug, Rachid Ahl Laamara
abstract: We investigate the energetic and thermodynamic performance of an interacting two-qubit system serving as both a quantum battery and a quantum Otto heat engine. The working medium is described by an anisotropic Heisenberg Hamiltonian supplemented by a dipolar interaction, a symmetric spin--orbit interaction, and an external magnetic field. Within a unified microscopic framework, we first analyze a coherent unitary charging protocol and characterize the resulting energy-storage performance through the ergotropy, anti-ergotropy, charging power, storage capacity, and $\ell_1$-norm of quantum coherence. We investigate the effects of the dipolar interaction, temperature, and magnetic field on these quantities. We then employ the same working medium in a quantum Otto cycle and study the absorbed and released heat, net work, and thermodynamic efficiency as functions of the magnetic-field modulation, dipolar interaction, and temperature bias. A direct comparison between the two protocols reveals a pronounced contrast in their response to the dipolar interaction. In the investigated parameter regime, increasing the dipolar interaction substantially enhances the maximum ergotropy and storage capacity of the quantum battery, whereas the maximum work extracted per Otto cycle decreases. The Otto efficiency exhibits a nonmonotonic dependence on the dipolar interaction while remaining below the Carnot bound. These results demonstrate that an enhancement of quantum energy-storage capability does not necessarily imply an enhancement of heat-to-work conversion. Our findings highlight the complementary nature of quantum batteries and quantum heat engines and show how microscopic spin interactions can   be used to control different forms of quantum energy conversion within   the same physical platform.
summary: This paper investigates an interacting two-qubit spin system used as both a quantum battery and a quantum heat engine. By analyzing the effects of dipolar interactions, the authors show that enhancing energy storage capability does not guarantee enhanced work extraction efficiency. This highlights the complementary and distinct nature of quantum energy storage and heat-to-work conversion processes.
main_problem: The study compares the energetic performance of a quantum battery (energy storage) versus a quantum Otto heat engine (heat-to-work conversion) in a single interacting spin system.
main_result: The research demonstrates a pronounced contrast: increasing a specific microscopic interaction (dipolar coupling) enhances the battery's energy storage capacity but decreases the maximum work extractable from the heat engine.
method: The authors analyze the system using theoretical quantum mechanics, calculating key thermodynamic and quantum coherence measures for both protocols.
model_or_system: The system is an interacting two-qubit spin system governed by an anisotropic Heisenberg Hamiltonian, supplemented by dipolar, spin-orbit, and external magnetic field interactions.
key_observables: Ergotropy, anti-ergotropy, storage capacity, net work, and thermodynamic efficiency.
important_parameters: Dipolar interaction strength, temperature bias, and external magnetic field strength.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the system can be modeled by the specified Hamiltonian and compares results derived from two distinct thermodynamic protocols.
figures_summary: Figures schematically represent the battery and Otto engine protocols on the two-qubit system, and tables/figures summarize the quantitative dependence of key observables on the dipolar interaction.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the model, analyzes the quantum battery protocol, investigates the quantum Otto cycle, directly compares the performance metrics, and concludes by contrasting the findings.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it uses a microscopic model to differentiate between two distinct forms of energy conversion (storage vs. work), providing insights into how local interactions control different thermodynamic pathways in quantum systems.
